A B S T R A C T

For the distributed flexible job shop scheduling problem (DFJSP), the existing researches have predominantly focused on operation sequence, machine selection and factory assignment, and assuming that the jobs have no priority. However, in real-world manufacturing systems, production scheduling with job priority is very common and is of concern to production managers. The paper presents a DFJSP with job priority (DFJSPJP) for the first time, aiming at minimizing the makespan, total energy consumption and the weighted average time of jobs with priority. A new memetic algorithm (NMA) is designed to solve the proposed DFJSPJP. In the proposed NMA, a well-designed chromosome encoding method (CEM) is constructed to obtain a high-quality initial population. An effective local search approach (LSO) is proposed to improve the NMA’s convergence speed and fully exploit its solution space. Computational experiments conducted confirm the effectiveness of the CEM and LSO, and show that the NMA is able to easily obtain better solutions for about 90 % of the tested 60 challenging problem instances compared to other three well-known algorithms, demonstrating its superior performance on both solution quality and computational efficiency. This research will provide a theoretical basis for considering job priority issues in distributed production environments and assist manufacturers in conducting accurate production scheduling, thereby reducing resource waste and time loss caused by unreasonable production plans.
1. Introduction

In recent years, with the rise of economic globalization and the increasing diverse demands of customers, manufacturing systems are shifting from traditional highly centralized environments to more flexible distributed settings to allocate production resources sensibly and enhance production efficiency. Distributed flexible job shop scheduling (DFJSP) [1–5] has emerged as a prominent research focus because of its practical relevance and significance for managers to make production decisions in manufacturing systems. DFJSP involves the strategic arrangement of jobs, factories, workshops, and machines to derive viable solutions [6–9], encompassing four key sub-problems: (1) allocating each job to a factory from a set of optional factories; (2) assigning each job to a workshop selected from the optional workshops within the corresponding factory; (3) allotting each job to a machine chosen from the optional machines within the corresponding workshop of factory; and (4) sequencing operations while adhering to constraints across factories, machines, and operations concurrently [10,11]. Undoubtedly, DFJSP poses a more challenging NP-hard conundrum compared to the traditional flexible job shop scheduling problem (FJSP) involving a single factory only [12–14].

Over the past few decades, DFJSP has attracted wide attention [15–18] from researchers due to its practical significance for decision-making by managers in manufacturing systems. Different researchers have extended this problem in various ways. So far, to the best of our-knowledge, all of the studies on DFJSP focused on operation sequence, machine selection and factory assignment, and assuming that the jobs have no priority. However, in real-world manufacturing systems, production scheduling that incorporates job priorities is a prevalent phenomenon and a key concern for production managers.

To thoroughly elucidate the practical application context of the distributed flexible job shop scheduling problem (DFJSP) with job priorities, this paper provides a detailed explanation through Fig. 1. Among them, Fig. 1(a) illustrates a typical distributed production workshop layout for industrial robots. Fig. 1(b) presents the main structure of an industrial robot, in which the base is the highest-priority component. As the foundational support structure of industrial robots, the base serves as the assembly reference for all other components. Its manufacturing progress directly influences the execution of downstream assembly processes and the delivery timeline of the overall equipment. Consequently, optimizing the production scheduling of high-priority tasks (such as the base) without affecting the overall project timeline has become an important issue that companies need to address to achieve efficient production.

According to the preferences of the production manager, the evalu ation results of these two approaches may be completely different.

• If the production manager only cares about the completion time, then the two solutions are the same; if the production manager only cares about the priority ofjob 5, the two solutions are also the same.

Therefore, it is very urgent and important to propose an effective algorithm to solve the DFJSPJP problem, in order to help production managers make efficient decisions when considering problems with different job priorities.

In this paper, a multi-objective DFJSPJP model is proposed, aiming at minimizing the makespan, total energy consumption and the weighted average time of jobs with priority. As far as we know, this is the first time job priorities have been studied in related literature. MAs, which integrate evolutionary algorithms with local search, have demonstrated promising performance in solving multi-objective DFJSPs. Motivated by this, we propose a new NMA to address the DFJSPJP we proposed. In the NMA, a well-designed chromosome encoding mechanism (CEM) is utilized to establish a high-quality initial population by fully leveraging the information and structure of DFJSPJP. An effective local search method (LSO) is proposed and integrated into the genetic algorithm to enhance its convergence speed and fully exploit the solution space. Experimental results on a diverse set of up to 60 benchmark instances from literature validate the effectiveness of the proposed NMA and its components (CEM and LSO).

2. Literature review
2.1. DFJSP related work

De Giovanni and Pezzella [19] were pioneers in the study of DFJSP, where tasks were allocated to multiple flexible manufacturing units fo concurrent processing. They developed an enhanced genetic algorithm (GA) incorporating greedy decoding and local search operators to tackle this challenge. Subsequently, a plethora of researchers have devised diverse approaches to address the DFJSP. Du et al. [20] set up a constraint programming model and developed a hybrid algorithm tha integrates a distribution estimation algorithm and variable neighbor hood search (VNS) to tackle the DFJSP, aiming to minimize the make span and crane transportation. Recognizing the decentralized nature of the DFJSP model, Li et al. [21] introduced a hybrid tabu search algo rithm with an optimization criterion and successfully applied it to a practical DFJSP scenario. Marzouki et al. [22] opted for a multi-agent system utilizing a meta-heuristic based on the forbidden search princi ple to optimize job assignments and factory scheduling, achieving commendable outcomes. Drawing inspiration from the collision princi ple in chemical reactions, Marzouki et al. [23] innovatively proposed a chemical reaction meta-heuristic algorithm for DFJSP optimization. Wu and Liu [24] formulated a mixed integer linear model for DFJSP and employed an enhanced differential evolutionary simulated annealing algorithm to pursue locally optimal solutions. Jiang et al. [25] intro duced an improved multi-objective decomposition evolutionary algo rithm to optimize energy-efficient DFJSP, aiming to minimize makespan and energy consumption. Chang and Liu [26] devised a hybrid GA incorporating a roulette encoding method to address job assignment challenges. Meng et al. [27] developed four mixed integer programming models and an efficient constraint programming model to solve the DFJSP, evaluating their efficacy through numerical experiments. They designed an energy regulation strategy to enhance algorithm perfor mance. Furthermore, various enhanced hybrid GAs have been widely presented to tackle the complexities of DFJSP [28]. Wang et al. [18] proposed an improved adaptive hybrid algorithm (IAHA) to tackle the distributed flexible job shop scheduling problem (DFJSP) in the contex of economic globalization and distributed manufacturing. The algorithm constructs a mathematical model for distributed factories, incorporate a dual-level encoding hybrid decoding rule, and employs an adaptive variable neighborhood search strategy to optimize cross-factory task allocation. Experimental results show that IAHA breaks multiple record and achieves optimal solutions in standard test cases involving 2 4 factories, highlighting its superior performance in solving DFJSP compared to existing methods.

2.2. Work related to job priority

In today’s increasingly complex manufacturing environment, it is inevitable to consider the priority of job processing. Processing highpriority jobs as soon as possible will benefit the subsequent assembly and transportation work in the entire factory. Production scheduling with job priorities is very common and is a matter of great concern for production managers. Therefore, many researchers have studied various scheduling problems based on job priorities to achieve better production scheduling solutions. Li et al. [35] proposed a highly efficient hybrid self-adaptive differential evolution algorithm (HSDE) with heuristic strategies. They studied the flexible job shop scheduling problem with outsourcing and job priorities, achieving good results. Li et al. [36] proposed a dual deep Q-network-based co-evolutionary algorithm (D2QCE) to address the distributed heterogeneous hybrid flow shop scheduling problem with multi-priority jobs (DHHFSP-MPJ). By balancing global and local search, knowledge-driven neighborhood structures, and energy-saving strategies, D2QCE significantly reduces weighted tardiness and energy consumption. Experiments demonstrate that D2QCE outperforms existing algorithms on 20 benchmark instances and a real-world case of large-scale equipment manufacturing, providing an efficient solution for engineering practices that consider priority, delivery constraints, and resource optimization in scheduling decisions.

From the above literature, it is evident that priority, as an important research area in the academic community, has been highly valued by many researchers. However, previous studies on distributed flexible job shops did not consider the issue ofjob priorities, which is actually one of the most common requirements in modern production scenarios. For example, in a batch of job orders, there are several jobs that need to be manufactured with priority. How should we handle such orders? Therefore, this paper innovatively studied the DFJSP considering job priorities, not only opening up a new research branch theoretically for future researchers, but also providing practical solutions for producers facing the DFJSP situations with job priority requirements.

4.2. Population initialization

A novel load balancing initialization rule has been developed based on the proposed CEM encoding operator with five levels. Initially, job priorities are randomly assigned and the job operations are sorted. The key concept is to prioritize operations of jobs with higher priority, assigning them to the same factory, workshop, and machine as the preceding operation to minimize inter-machine, inter-workshop, and inter-factory transportation. Alternatively, if needed, cumulative processing times for machines, workshops, and factories are calculated. Subsequently, machines, workshops, and factories are selected for each operation in sequence based on the minimum cumulative processing time. The specific steps are outlined below, with the core pseudocode of the initialization method detailed in Algorithm 1.
Step 1. Set the total job level as "pri" and randomly assign priorities to the jobs.

5. Experiments and analysis

The proposed NMA for the DFJSPJP was executed in MATLAB R2020a and run on a computer with an Intel Core i5 2.9 GHz and 16 GB RAM. To test the performance of NMA, three experiments were carried out. Firstly, the key parameters of four algorithms, including NMA, were determined through Taguchi experiments [46,47], and NMA was compared with the other three algorithms. Then, verify the validity of the operators proposed in this paper. Finally, the superior performance of NMA algorithm is proved by comparing with other algorithms. Each benchmark instance was run 10 times to reduce randomness in the experimental results.
5.1. Constructing the DFSPJP benchmarks

In order to evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed NMA in dealing with the DFJSPJP model, a set of 60 DFJSPJP benchmark instances (named DDs 01–60) were created based on established examples of the traditional DFJSPJP standard. These instances are categorized into three sizes: small benchmark instances (DDs 01–20), medium benchmark instances (DDs 21 40), and large benchmark instances (DDs 41 60). In all the instances developed, the machine’s power consumption of each processing unit time is randomly set between 5 and 15; the unit transport time between different factories, workshops, and machines are defined as 20, 10, and $^ { 5 , }$ respectively; the unit energy consumption resulting from unit transportation time is set to 10. The generated benchmark instances DDs 01–60 are available for download from the following website: https://github.com/Heao1234/Heao.
5.2. Performance evaluation metrics

Three widely used metrics were chosen to test the performance of the proposed algorithm and its operators, including the C-metric [48,49], inverted generational distance (IGD) [50,51] and hypervolume metric (HV) [52]. For the C-metric, the larger the value of C (A, B), the better the solution set ofA, and vice versa; for the IGD, the lower the IGD value, the better the algorithm performance, and vice versa; and for the HV, the higher the HV value, the better the algorithm performance, and vice versa. More specific descriptions can be seen from the corresponding references.
5.3. Parameter settings

Different parameters affect the overall performance of the algorithm, so it is necessary to tune the settings of the key parameters. In this paper, the key parameters include population size (NP), crossover probability (CP), mutation probability (MP), and local search probability (LP). Here, the Taguchi experimental method is employed to calibrate the level of each key parameter in NMA and the three competitive algorithms. Specifically, we designed an orthogonal experiment containing 16 parameter combinations, as shown in columns 2–5 of Table 4. The four levels for each parameter are set as follows: NP = [60,90,120,150], CP = [0.40, 0.50, 0.60, 0.70], MP = [0.10, 0.20, 0.30, 0.40], and LP = [0.20, 0.30, 0.40, 0.50]. Three instances were selected for the experiment including small-scale (DD01), medium-scale (DD 32) and large-scale (DD 54), and the IGD was selected as the evaluation index for the experimental results.
5.3.2. Parameter calibration of the comparison algorithms

In this paper, NNIA [53], NSGA-II [54], and NSGA-III [5,55] were selected as comparison algorithms. The main reasons for choosing these three comparison algorithms are as follows: (1) all of the NNIA, NSGA-II, NSGA-III, and NMA are based on traditional genetic algorithms, so they have similar frameworks; (2) all these algorithms use the non-dominated sorting method to deal with multi-objective problems; and (3) all these algorithms are classical algorithms are usually used as the baseline algorithms to verify the effectiveness of the newly proposed multi-objective algorithms.
To ensure the fairness of the experiment, the Taguchi experiment is also used to calibrate the key parameters of the NNIA, NSGA-II and NSGA-III based on three instances (DD 01, DD 32, and DD 54).

5.6. Time complexity analysis

The computational complexity of our proposed NMA (new memetic algorithm) is primarily influenced by four key components: objective function evaluation, fast non-dominated sorting, crowding distance calculation, and the local search operation. For a population of size N and M objective functions, the complexity of assessing the objective functions is O (MN). The most computationally demanding steps are the fast non-dominated sorting and the crowding distance calculation. Both steps involve sorting individuals for each objective function, resulting in a complexity of O (MN²). The complexity of local search operations is closely related to the complexity of operational exchange method (OEM) and machine exchange method (MEM). The OEM has a complexity of O (K⋅T1⋅T2), where K represents the number of individuals selected from the first level of the population through fast non-dominated sorting, and T1 and T2 are random integers selected from 1 to $N _ { c p }$ (the number of critical blocks on the critical path). The MEM, on the other hand, has a complexity of $O \left( K { \cdot } L \tau _ { } \right) ,$ where L1 is a random integer selected from 1 to $N _ { c p } .$ Combining these components, the overall computational complexity of the NMA is O (max $\lbrace M N ^ { 2 } ;$ , K⋅T1⋅T2, K⋅L1}).

In this paper, we studied the DFJSPJP considering the completion time, total energy consumption, and the weighted average time of job priorities. The DFJSPJP can assist production managers in dealing with scheduling issues involving job priorities, which are widespread in the real world but have been completely neglected in theoretical research. We propose an effective NMA to solve the DFJSPJP. In the NMA, an CEM was constructed by sufficiently making use of the information and structure of the DFJSPJP, which can guarantee the NMA to obtain a high-quality initial population; and a local search operator (LSO) with two methods is designed to enhance the convergence speed of the NMA.
